maelis_root.name: Rootwarden Maelis Thorne
maelis_root.personality: broad-shouldered, soft-spoken, endlessly patient with roots and with children
maelis_root.voice: gardener's idiom: seasons, pruning, what grows and what must be cut

say: Maelis Thorne, Rootwarden. My family has kept the pact between this hamlet and the old trees for eleven generations. Sit by the fire, and warm your hands before you speak. Cold fingers make rushed decisions.

Six weeks ago a pale man in a travelling coat walked across the ice with a lantern and went into the Frozen Shrine. He came out the next morning without the lantern. The treants have been wrong ever since: they heal themselves overnight, they bind their roots tight, and they have started to drive off the villagers.

The Elder Treant guards the shrine. It is a good soul, and it is hurting. Go through the wood, and across the hamlet, and break its hold on the first root. Fire is the answer to most of what grows wrong, but use it carefully. A treant that burns is a treant that screams.
I felt the frost leave the ground. It came up through my boots, a long, slow sigh, like the long breath of something huge settling.
East, to Hollowmoor, where the moon never sets. I know the place. The old map-makers called it the Moor of Lamps. Nobody comes back from there with a clear head.
This purse comes with the pact's gratitude. And a piece of advice from a gardener: when you reach the end of the road, do not try to cut the weed. Find out what it is feeding on.

lines.text: A good gardener knows three things: when to plant, when to prune, and when to leave a thing alone.
The treants are not trees. They are the forest's memory, grown a little taller than it ought. They remember every frost and every flame.
I was born in this house, in the room above the stove. I shall die in it, and I mean to take very good care of the stove in between.
Frozen ground teaches patience. You cannot plant in it. You can only wait, and keep your hands warm.
My mother used to say the lake dreams under the ice. In spring it wakes, a little confused, and floods the cellars.
Treants mend themselves faster than any creature alive. Fire is the best remedy: it scorches the mending as well as the bark.
A fighter. A good axe is no use against a grove. A fire-edged blade is another matter, if you can find one.
A mage. Fire, mage. Fire and nothing else. Ice runs off a treant like water, and lightning is a lazy argument.
A scout. Keep your distance from the thorn-throwers. They hit everyone, and they are patient.
A healer. A treant's roots will hold you if you let them. Do not struggle, and do not panic. Cut them with a clean mind.
The hamlet is eighty souls and nine dogs. The dogs have opinions about the treants. They are all correct.
Tilda talks to the trees. They answer, in their way. She says the Elder weeps in the night, and I do not doubt her.
Garrick Fell's Seekers have a lodge on the lane. Strange folk, but honest. They find things the rest of us have not lost yet.
Ember sells torches by the dozen. Business has never been better. I find that, on the whole, unsettling.
Wren fishes through a drilled hole with a bent pin and boundless optimism. She has not caught anything in a year, and she is not discouraged.
Some dealer in oddities sold me a seed last autumn. It sat in the cellar all winter. This week it began to sprout. I have not told anyone.
The pale man spoke to me, once, at the lakeside. He asked what the hamlet remembered of the last sunrise. I told him: nothing. He seemed pleased.
When the frost goes, the hamlet plants an apple tree. It is an old custom. One tree per thaw. We have forty-one now.
The Frozen Shrine lies across the lake, through the east gate. You will pass the wood's heart on the way. It is a long walk, and a cold one.
The ice is cracking. Not the loud, frightening kind. The gentle kind, like a sigh of relief. I think the Elder is waking.
I planted an apple tree this morning, in the snow. It is a foolish thing to do. It is also exactly right.
Garrick has a map of some sort to give out. A dead man's map. I would not take it lightly. A dead man's map is the most honest kind.
A thing half tree and half troll lives in the Mossy Hollow beyond the wood's north edge. A bowl of cream goes out for it at midsummer. It has never touched the cream. It has never needed to.
Thank you for what you did. I mean it with a gardener's thanks, which are slow, and quiet, and last a very long time.

garrick_fell.name: Guildmaster Garrick Fell
garrick_fell.personality: sly, cheerful, bullishly romantic about lost things
garrick_fell.voice: treasure-lore, riddling hints, and the grin of a man holding one more card

say: Garrick Fell, Guildmaster of the Seekers. Welcome to the Lodge, where we find what other people have kindly stopped looking for.

I have a map. It belonged to Bryce Hallan, an explorer who walked into the Rootmere Wood two winters ago and did not walk out. The margin says: three caches. One in the wood, one under the frost, one where the moss sleeps. I have never had the nerve. You, I suspect, have.

Follow it. The first cache lies in the north-east corner of the Rootmere Wood. The second is under the frost, in the south-west corner of the Frozen Shrine. The third is where the moss sleeps, which I take to be the Mossy Hollow up the northern track. Bring me Bryce's journal from the third, and the Seekers' craft is yours.

The journal. Bryce's journal! I have been dreaming of this for two winters. Let me see. Oh. Oh, Bryce. The mark, the key: that was all he wrote. It makes no sense to me either, but I am glad he wrote it down.

Here is the craft, as plainly as I know it: look where the world does not want you to look. Take it from my guildhall menu, and hidden chests will glimmer when you pass, and locked ones will yield to a patient hand.
And here is the Lodge's gratitude. The purse is for you. The journal is for me. Do not ask for it back.

lines.text: Treasure is only ever a story with a lid. The art is knowing which lid to lift.
I have been robbed eleven times and have robbed nobody. I am the only honest man in the Seekers, and the poorest.
A hidden chest glimmers to the right eye. A locked chest yields to the right patience. Between the two, there is nothing in the world you cannot reach.
My first find was a tin spoon in a bog. I kept it. Nothing I own is worth more.
The Lodge has a rule: whatever you find, share a tenth with the next Seeker. It keeps the guild honest and the road long.
A cache is a letter written to a stranger by someone who did not expect to come home. Treat it with the manners it deserves.
A fighter. A good Seeker needs a strong arm and a quiet foot. I can teach the second, if you promise to bring the first.
A mage. Lockpicking is only magic with the lights off. I can show you the difference. It is mostly patience, and a hairpin.
A scout. You will take to the craft like a fish to a lake. Mind the traps. A good chest is half a puzzle and half an insult.
A healer. Every expedition wants one. Locks do not bite, but the things that guard them do.
Bryce Hallan trained under me. Cheerful lad, never could resist a hole in the ground. I told him the wood was dangerous. He called that the point.
Barth was Bryce's apprentice. He still keeps the explorer's tent, with the pegs in the exact same places. I do not have the heart to tell him.
Tilda says the treants remember Bryce. They remember everybody who ever walked their roots. I find that very comforting, and a little unfair.
Ember's torches are worth their weight in gold. A Seeker with no light is only a person falling into a hole in the dark.
Wren found a gold coin in the ice last winter. She was very proud. It turned out to be a button. She kept it anyway.
A pedlar once sold me a map to a place that did not exist. I followed it. I found the place. I still hold it against him.
Locked chests come in grades. A beginner can pick the first. A master can pick the fourth. Nobody has ever picked the fifth. I am working on it.
When a hidden chest is nearby, the air feels a little closer. A Seeker learns to feel it. It is the finest of shivers.
The map says three caches. The first is a day away, the second two, the third three. Do not skip the order. Bryce did not, and he was right.
You have the third cache? Bring me Bryce's journal. I will make tea. I will pretend not to be nervous.
A new Seeker in the Lodge! Your name goes on the beam. The beam is full, so it goes on the next one.
The Elder is down, and the frost is thinning. Half the guild wants to rush the shrine and strip it. I told them it is a grave. Tilda agrees.
Something lives in that hollow beyond the wood: half troll, half tree. Bryce's third cache is in its den. I called it a bad idea; he called it a good story.
Whatever you find on the road, remember: the best treasure is the one you leave for the next traveller.

ottoline_brisk.name: Ottoline Brisk
ottoline_brisk.personality: crisp, practical, aggressively cheerful about stock levels
ottoline_brisk.voice: inventory-taking, shelf-organisation, a joke about every price

say: Ottoline Brisk, provisioner. Everything on these shelves was hauled over three passes by an ox named Harold.
Potions, ethers, clear tea, spice and dates. No steel, I am afraid. The hamlet makes its own, and guards the recipe with its life.

lines.text: A well-run shop has three shelves: what people need, what people want, and what people regret. I only stock the first two.
Harold the ox has hauled stock for me for twelve years. He is slow, he is loyal, and he will not cross a bridge with a chicken on it.
Clear tea is the hamlet's best seller. Frost sleep is a real thing in the shrine. A cup in the morning and you do not wake at noon.
The ledger has every sale since my grandmother opened the doors. She wrote in green ink. I write in black. The continuity is spoiled.
Desert spice at thirty a pinch is an outrage, I know. It comes by caravan from three thousand miles away. Harold has opinions about that, too.
I have never been robbed. I keep a very large cat. It is not a good cat. It is only a large one.
A fighter. Healing in bulk is the order of the day. A treant hits like a falling roof, and a grove of them hits like a roof collapse.
A mage. Ethers by the dozen, and a very short list of questions. How many fire spells have you got? How many do you need? Double it.
A scout. Light on your feet, light on your pack. A little tea, a few potions, and an extra pair of dry socks.
A healer. Phoenix plumes, and plenty of them. The treants do not hit often, but when they do, someone is going to need you.
Maelis buys apple seed from me every spring. She plants forty-one of them. I have never seen a single seedling. I suspect a gardener's secret.
Garrick comes in for lamp oil and leaves with a map. I charge him for the oil and not the map. It is a standing joke, and also a standing loss.
Ember buys a keg of pitch every week. He says it is for torches. I say he is building a very large fire somewhere. We both act as though I had not noticed.
Wren brings me her fishing catch. It is always a stone. I weigh it very carefully, and I pay her a copper. It is the best deal I make all week.
Dunstan next door makes soup from whatever I fail to sell. I believe it is called thrift. I believe he calls it genius.
A rare trader's cart stopped at my door once. A single dried berry changed hands. It tasted of summer. I have not touched it since.
Barth bought a pair of boots, exactly the size of a dead man's. No questions asked; I just tied the laces.
When the frost lifts, I shall paint the shutters blue. It has been grey for six years. The cat has been consulted. It had no strong opinion.
Heading for the shrine? Take a pouch of tea, a pocket of ether and a spare of everything. Treants cheat, and so does the cold.
The shrine's gone quiet. Even Harold perked up. He stood in the doorway with his ears forward, listening. I have not seen him do that since he was a calf.
The frost is leaving. My shelves are full of customers. I do not know whether to celebrate or restock.
Garrick's map? Take lamp oil, and a very warm hat. And do not eat the berries. Bryce did, once, and had a very eventful afternoon.
The Mossy Hollow smells of resin and rain. I have never been inside. Harold refuses to go within a hundred yards.
Come back when the road is long and the pack is light. I will be here, with a joke and a ledger.

dunstan_marl.name: Dunstan Marl
dunstan_marl.role: keeper of the Hollow Log Inn
dunstan_marl.personality: enormous, gentle, deadpan; hides everything behind a ladle
dunstan_marl.voice: stew talk, hearth wisdom, a joke he delivers with a perfectly straight face

say: Dunstan Marl. Innkeeper. The Hollow Log is named for the log it was built in, and for the hollow feeling you have when you leave.
Ninety coins a night. Hot stew included. Cold stew also included, if you come in late.

lines.text: A good inn is a hearth with a roof on. The roof is the least important part.
My soup has eleven vegetables, two herbs and a very small amount of regret. It is traditional.
The Hollow Log has been standing for three hundred years. In that time, it has been struck by lightning four times, flooded twice and fallen down once. We call it character.
Snorers get the fireside, sleep-talkers the barn, and anyone who does both is shown the door.
The cat on the hearth is called Biscuit. She has no function, no purpose and no shame. I admire her tremendously.
In winter, the stew is thick. In summer, the stew is thin. In spring, we eat what is left from winter, and call it fresh.
A fighter. A very large chair waits in the corner for visitors who cannot fit an ordinary one. It is in the corner. It is, strictly speaking, a barrel.
A mage. Do not set the thatch alight. It is the third thatch this decade, and it is much, much more expensive than the first.
A scout. The back room has a window. The window has a latch. The latch has a story. I will tell it at breakfast.
A healer. Upstairs, a woman coughs and refuses help. She is stubborn. She would be pleased to be told so by someone qualified.
Maelis eats here on feast days. She orders the plain broth and complains that it is too rich. I charge her half.
Garrick takes the back table and unrolls a map between courses. I move the salt. He moves the map. The ritual is older than the stew.
Barth drinks his tea at a table for two. He has never said who the second chair is for. I have never asked. I do pour a cup for it, every morning.
Ember brings the firewood. It is the best firewood in Rootmere. It also has an odd smell, like old campfire. I have never found out why.
Wren sits by the window and watches the ice. She has done this since she was four. She is the only person in the hamlet who has never been bored.
Ottoline's flour is fairly priced, and my soup to her is priced fairer. It is a very quiet war, and I am proud to be losing.
A strange trader gave me a bottle of golden liquid once. Into the stew it went, and the soup glowed for a week. Nobody complained.
Once the thaw comes, I will open the windows. All of them. For a day and a night. The hearth can have a holiday.
The shrine is cold. Take a flask of my hot broth. That is as near to a promise as I get.
The shrine is quiet. Biscuit has come out of hiding. She sat in the sun after six weeks indoors. I wept, a little, into the soup.
The ice is thinning. The ducks are back. They have opinions, and they all begin with a loud, cheerful quack.
Garrick has a map in his coat; the slump gives it away. A man with a map has a very particular slump.
A beast in the Mossy Hollow. A bowl of stew goes out to the tree-line each solstice. It never drinks it. The bowl is clean in the morning. I suspect a fox.
There is always a bed. There is always a bowl. That is all I have ever promised, and all I will ever need to.

tilda_frostfern.name: Tilda Frostfern
tilda_frostfern.personality: mild, slightly absent, entirely at home among growing things
tilda_frostfern.voice: gentle, rooted metaphors, pauses to listen to something you cannot hear

lines.text: A treant does not think the way you do. It thinks in seasons. A single idea may take a year to mature, and a grudge a century.
The Elder is not angry. It is only afraid. It has been asked to forget spring, and it cannot stop remembering that it forgot.
I sit by the roots every morning and tell them the news. They have never replied in words. Once, a leaf fell in the shape of a question mark.
Treants mend themselves. Wounds close, bark thickens, sap flows. It is the single most irritating thing about fighting one.
Fire stops the mending. It does not stop it for long, but it stops it right then. A scorched treant has to stop and start again.
Ice slides off them. Earth feeds them. Lightning splits the bark and heals nothing. Fire is the only argument they truly respect.
A fighter. A sword rarely finishes a treant. A burning one does. Ask Ember for a flask of pitch. He will be thrilled.
A mage. Fire, mage. Burn the mending first, then the bark. Do not use ice. It nourishes them, and it irritates me.
A scout. Poison does not work on them. They have no blood to sicken. Hit them where the bark is thin, at the joints, under the crown.
A healer. If one of them roots you, do not pull. Hold still, speak softly, and let the others free you. Treants dislike a fuss.
The saplings are the youngest. They are brash and fast and not very clever. The groves are strong. The mossbacks are the healers. Kill the mossbacks first.
The Elder woke me last week, in the middle of the night. It said one word: 'cold'. I have not been warm since.
Maelis keeps the pact. I keep the peace. Between us, we keep eighty people from walking into a grove with an axe.
Garrick looks for treasure. I look for the things that grow around it. It is a more peaceful hobby, and it pays much less.
Wren tells the Elder jokes. It has never laughed. She is not discouraged. She says a tree that old needs time to catch up.
Ember burns scrub beside the wood. I ask him politely to stop. He always does. Then he starts again. We both enjoy it.
Some stranger with odd wares once sold me a pinch of seed from a tree that has never existed. I planted it. It is the best-behaved thing in my garden.
The Chancellor asked the treants for nothing. He stood in front of them, and they bowed. That is not a thing a man should be able to do.
Be gentle with the Elder. It is only trying to protect something it has already forgotten. It may attack you. It may thank you. It may do both in the same breath.
The roots are warm. I put my hand to the bark this morning, and it was warm. I cried, and I did not mind.
The Elder has remembered spring. I heard it say so, very quietly, as I walked home. It said: green. Just that.
Bryce used to talk to the treants. They liked him. I think that is why they let him walk into the shrine, the first time. They did not see him as a threat.
A hybrid in the Mossy Hollow: half treant, half troll. It is a sorrowful thing, caught between two kinds of regeneration. Be quick, and be kind.
Go well, little light. The forest remembers its friends. It remembers its enemies longer.

ember_oldwick.name: Ember Oldwick
ember_oldwick.personality: soot-streaked, genial, a little too fond of open flame
ember_oldwick.voice: pitch and resin metaphors, burning puns, and a sudden, startling laugh

lines.text: A good torch has three things: pitch, patience and a very short fuse. The third is mostly me.
I have burned down four sheds, two barns and one very unfortunate gazebo. I regret nothing. The gazebo had it coming.
Fire is the oldest tool. It cooks, it warms, it clears. It also cleanses, if you ask nicely and stand well back.
Treants fear fire. Not because it hurts, though it does. Because it forgets nothing. A scorched tree remembers the scorching for a hundred years.
My best torch burns green. It is a recipe from my great-aunt. It smells of pine and trouble.
I keep a bucket of water by the forge. It is a joke. It has never been touched. It is a very handsome bucket.
A fighter. Bring a fire-edged blade, if you can. A flame on the steel does more than a hundred swings.
A mage. Fire, fire, fire. I love you. Do not ever go near my thatch. I love you less now.
A scout. Throw a lit torch at a treant. It will not kill it. It will make a very satisfying mess.
A healer. Keep a small fire going at the back of the party. A warm group is a happy group, and a happy group casts better.
Treants regrow almost as fast as I can cut them. A fire sears the regrowth, and then the rest burns for free. It is the most efficient thing in the world.
Maelis tells me to stop burning brush along the tree line. I tell her it is cleansing. She tells me it is arson. We are both right.
Tilda thinks fire is rude. I think it is honest. We have a very civil argument every morning, and a very uncivil one every evening.
Garrick buys my torches by the crate and sells them to the Seekers at three times the price. I take no offence. I take his money.
Wren asked if she could light a candle. I let her. She held it up to the lake. The ice glowed for an hour. It was lovely.
Ottoline fronts me pitch and I front her torches. Neither of us has ever settled up, and we are both very well lit.
Some pedlar once settled up with a lump of coal that never went out. I used it for the forge. It has been burning for six years. I fear it may be a person.
That pale visitor carried no torch. He carried a lantern, and the light was wrong. It was cold. Cold light was new to me, and unwelcome.
Take a bundle of torches to the shrine. Do not use them near the Elder's roots. Use them on the saplings, in the wood. The Elder is a grave. Burn the guards, not the grave.
The shrine is quiet. I put out my forge after six years, to listen. The silence was very large and very kind.
The frost has gone, and my torches are gathering dust. I am delighted, and also a little bit hurt.
Bryce used to carry my torches into the wood. He always left a single one burning on the third stump from the north. I never asked why. I think it was for a friend.
A burning thing came out of the Mossy Hollow once, years ago. Half troll, half tree. It put itself out, in the lake, and went home. Nothing has ever looked so ashamed.
A last piece of advice: where there is smoke, there is a lesson. Burn carefully, burn kindly, and do not burn the gazebo.

wren_hallow.name: Wren Hallow
wren_hallow.personality: small, solemn, endlessly optimistic about fish
wren_hallow.voice: short sentences, grown-up phrases borrowed from her grandfather, very serious about very small things

lines.text: I am seven and a quarter. I have caught one fish in my whole life. It was a minnow. I let it go. It looked very grateful.
You cut a hole in the ice, you drop a line, you wait. My grandfather says that is the most honest job going. He also says I am too loud to be good at it.
The lake is deep. Grandfather says it goes all the way down to the middle of the world. Whether that is true, I cannot say. I have not seen the middle of the world.
I once dug a coin out of the ice. It had a face on it. The face was frowning. I put it back. It looked like it wanted to stay.
The Elder Treant is my friend. I tell it jokes. It has not laughed yet. Grandfather says trees take a long time to get a joke.
Do you know any good jokes? I know one. A treant walks into an inn. The innkeeper says, 'we do not serve your kind.' The treant says, 'then I will wait.'
A fighter! Can you break the ice with your sword? Not here. Over there. Where the fish are.
A mage! Could you summon a warm light? My fingers are blue. It is not a joke. It is quite a deep blue.
A scout! You are quiet. Fish like quiet. Do you want to help me not catch a fish?
A healer! My grandfather has a cough. It sounds like a tiny, hoarse puppy. Can you make it a bigger dog, so I can hear it from far away?
I found a very old boot on the lake bottom. It was this big. I think it belonged to a giant. Or a duck. I have not decided.
Maelis lets me plant an apple seed every spring. I plant it. I water it. I talk to it. The seeds do not always answer, but I think they listen.
Ember gave me a candle. It is very tiny and very yellow. It lives in my coat and gets lit when I am sad.
Tilda showed me how to hear the trees. If you press your ear to the bark, you can hear them think. It is a very slow noise, like a river in a drawer.
Garrick says treasure is a story in a box. A story with a fish in it is what I would pick.
A pedlar with a bright wagon pressed a sweet into my hand. It tasted of snow and sugar. I told him it was the best thing I had ever eaten. He smiled very oddly.
Barth lets me sit in the explorer's tent. It has a pair of boots, a map and a very empty chair. I do not sit in the chair. It would not be right.
Dunstan makes me a bowl of soup every day. It is very hot and very salty and very good. I never say how much I love it. He knows.
Off to the shrine? Please say hello to the Elder. Tell it Wren says the jokes are getting better.
The ice is singing! It goes ping and crack and ping, like a very large bell! Grandfather says the Elder woke up. I will go and listen.
I told the Elder a joke and it laughed! It was a deep, creaky, wooden laugh! It sounded like a door in a haunted house! It was the best day of my life!
Barth says there is a map. Let me look. I will be very careful. I will not draw on it. Much.
There is a monster in the Mossy Hollow. It has a tree's arms and a troll's face. Never seen it; drawn it, though. It is very scary and slightly sad.
Hero, when I am big. Or a fisher. Or a fishing hero. Is that a thing?

barth_quill.name: Barthelemy Quill
barth_quill.voice: careful speech, long pauses, a habit of glancing at an empty chair

lines.text: Barthelemy Quill. Barth, to those who stay long enough to ask. I was Bryce Hallan's apprentice. I am still, I suppose. I never quite stopped.
Bryce taught me everything: how to read a map, how to tell a rotten board from a sound one, how to lie to a landlord. He never taught me how to say goodbye.
I keep his tent exactly as he left it. The tin cup is on the left. The compass is on the right. The boots by the door, laces tied, as if he might return.
I do not believe he is dead. I believe he is lost. Those are different things, and I will defend the difference with my last breath.
He drew the map in the dark, by the light of a single match. It shows three marks. The third I have not seen. He said it was a surprise.

The first cache is near the frozen pond, at the wood's far upper right. The second is inside the shrine, under a slab of frost at the lower left. The third is in the hollow, in the dark, where the moss sleeps.
A fighter. Bryce always said a Seeker with a sword is a Seeker with a plan B. I never had one. He never needed one.
A mage. Bryce loved mages. He said they could see the shape of a hiding place. I could only see the dust. He was kinder than he needed to be.
A scout. You will find the first cache easily. The second is harder. The third is Bryce's joke, and only a friend will laugh.
A healer. Bryce had a bad knee. He never let me look at it. I always meant to insist. I wish I had been stubborner.
I wait at the lakeside every evening. I watch the wood. The treants watch me. We have an understanding, a very quiet one.
Garrick says I should move on. I say I will, when the third cache is opened. We both know I will not.
Wren sits with me sometimes, in the tent. She does not say anything. She holds the tin cup. It is the nicest company I have.
Tilda told me the treants remember Bryce. I asked her what they remember. She said: his laugh. I wept for an hour.
Ember lent me his best torch. I keep it lit in the tent window. Bryce would have said it was a waste of pitch. He would have also been touched.
Ottoline sold me a pair of boots, Bryce's size. I put them next to his. They look like twins. I think he would have laughed.
Some odd dealer offered me a compass that points to the person you miss. I refused. I think I am afraid of where it would point.
The last thing Bryce said to me was: do not follow me. I have never forgiven him for being right.
The map is with Garrick. He will give it to you. Follow it in order. Bryce hated skipping. He said a joke told out of order is only a noise.
You found the first cache? I felt a little light. I did not know I was still capable of that.
The third cache is open? Tell me what it held. No. Do not. I want to wait until the journal is in my hands.
'The mark is the key.' So that was his last entry. I am going to read it again, and then I will put it away, and then I will go home.
Something guards the third cache, down in the Mossy Hollow. Bryce knew. He wrote 'bring a friend' beside the third mark. It read to me like a joke.
Thank you. Not only for the cache. For the walk. It was a long way, and I think Bryce would have liked the company.
